To receive.

examples.text: The company took in more than forty million euros last year.

glosses: To receive and properly absorb or comprehend.

examples.text: The news is a lot to take in right now.
I was so sleepy that I hardly took in any of the lecture.

At the final whistle, it was just like old times as those thousands of Leicester supporters stayed in their seats for the trophy celebration to take in scenes that will live with them forever while the Chelsea end was a scene of desolation before it became a sea of deserted red seats.

glosses: To enjoy or appreciate.

examples.text: I'm just going to sit on a bench and take in the scenery.
Just relax and take in the fresh ocean air.

glosses: To allow a person or an animal to live in one's home.

examples.text: take in a stray cat

glosses: To receive (goods) into one's home for the purpose of processing for a fee.

examples.text: In hard times, some women would take in washing and others dressmaking repairs.

glosses: To shorten (a garment) or make it smaller.

examples.text: Try taking the skirt in a little around the waist.

glosses: To attend a showing of.

examples.text: take in a show
take in a movie

glosses: To deceive; to hoodwink.

examples.text: Their grandma lost thousands of dollars because she was taken in by scammers.
She liked and trusted everybody, which was the reason why she was so popular, and so often taken in.

glosses: To tighten (a belaying rope).
To subscribe to home delivery of.

examples.text:
[James Whiteside:] May I ask what newspaper you take in? [John Jolly:] I take in no newspaper.
[James Whiteside:] Well, then, what newspapers do you read? [John Jolly:] I am glad to see any of them.

glosses: To reef.

examples.text: The second mate holds on to the main top-gallant sail until a heavy sea is shipped, and washes over the forecastle as though the whole ocean had come aboard; when a noise further aft shows that that sail, too, is taking in.

glosses: To arrest (a person).

examples.text: The police took in the suspect.

glosses: Llevar deliberadamente a alguno a creer lo que no es cierto.

examples.text: Levantó los ojos sin miedo alguno, riendo de estas palabras. El señor acostumbraba a engañarla con bromas inverosímiles. Bien decía su padre que los Febrer eran unos caballeros serios como jueces, pero de eterno buen humor. Iba a burlarse otra vez de ella, lo mismo que cuando le hablaba de la novia de barro guardada en su torre, que había estado esperándole miles de años.

glosses: Dicho de un efecto sensorial, llevar a inferencias inexactas acerca de lo que le da origen; producir la ilusión de los sentidos.

examples.text: [L]a cruz se sale del quadro como si fuera corpórea, tanto que llega a engañar la vista.

glosses: Faltar a la fidelidad conyugal, cometer adulterio.

examples.text: En La Burguesa de Orleans, un fabliau, la mujer que trama engañar a su marido con su amante es descubierta por su criada, lo que resulta extraño puesto que ésta suele ser siempre fiel a su señora y cómplice de sus engaños.

glosses: Desviar la atención para hacer una sensación más llevadera.

examples.text: A nosotros casi no nos daban de comer. Engañábamos el hambre con agua. Víctor tenia la cara llena de moretones y un ojo cerrado por la hinchazón.

glosses: A glossy, resinous material used as a surface coating; either a natural exudation of certain trees, or a solution of nitrocellulose in alcohol, etc.

examples.text: Had he deemed it "wisest, best," Mr. O'Donagough was not without the means of furnishing a splendid mansion in very showy style, and yet not leaving a single morsel of lacker, or or-molu, unpaid for.
It is a solvent for nitrocellulose and vinyl chloride-acetate resins and may function as an antiblush agent in lacquers.
Cellosolves are used as solvents for lacquers, for sealing cellophane wrapping, and in hydraulic-brake fluid.

In place of traditional methods in which materials such as gesso, yellow ocher, powdered earth, liquid glue, and Japan tallow were used to obtain a gloss, and transparent lacquer was rubbed into the wood to protect it, materials such as artificially produced varoids and lacquer came into widespread use.

glosses: To apply a lacquer to something or to give something a smooth, glossy finish.
A clear or translucent liquid coating composed of resin dissolved in a solvent, which dries by evaporation to form a hard, protective, and typically glossy finish.
Anything resembling such a coating; a glossy appearance.

examples.text: the varnish of the holly and ivy

glosses: A deceptively showy appearance.

examples.text: And set a double varnish on the fame / The Frenchman gave you.

glosses: A passenger train, probably derived from the varnished passenger cars used at one time.

examples.text: Every transcontinental but two settled on the simple articulated for freight service, and all of them coupled their varnish to the 4-8-4.

glosses: To apply varnish.
To cover up with varnish.
To make something superficially or deceptively attractive

examples.text: varnish the report

glosses: To gloss over a defect.

examples.text: [...] Go love thy infant; love thy wood-chopper: be good-natured and modest: have that grace; and never varnish your hard, uncharitable ambition with this incredible tenderness for black folk a thousand miles off. Thy love afar is spite at home.
